title: Real-Time: Polling, SSE, WebSockets
subtitle: Watch one chat message reach a user who never asked for it, using four different ways to let a server speak first.
learn: Why plain HTTP cannot push, and how short and long polling fake it
How Server-Sent Events and WebSockets keep one connection open
When to pick polling, SSE or WebSockets
Why connection gateways are stateful and what that does to scaling
How a message crosses gateways through a pub/sub bus, and what happens when a gateway dies

steps.title: The server has news, the client is silent
steps.body: Alice sends Bob a chat message. The server now has news for Bob, but Bob's app has not asked for anything. Plain HTTP only works one way: the client asks and the server answers. A server cannot start the conversation. So how does Bob's screen update without him refreshing? In this lesson we assume 100,000 connected users.
steps.idea: Plain HTTP is ask-then-answer, so real-time needs a trick or a different protocol.
steps.caption: Bob is idle; the news is waiting on the server.

steps.title: Ask again every few seconds
steps.body: The simplest fix is short polling: Bob's app asks 'anything new?' every 5 seconds. It works with any server and cache. The cost is waste. 100,000 users polling every 5 s is 20,000 requests per second, and almost all come back empty. A new message also waits half the interval on average, about 2.5 s, before Bob sees it. Each poll is a short-lived HTTP request, not a held-open connection.
steps.idea: Short polling is very simple, but it wastes requests and delays messages by half the poll interval on average.
steps.caption: Most polls come back empty.

steps.title: Ask, and the server waits
steps.body: Long polling cuts the waste. If there is nothing new, the server does not answer. It holds the request open, often up to 30 seconds, and replies the moment a message arrives. Then Bob's app asks again. A message could slip through the gap between requests, so each request carries the id of the last message seen and the server replays anything newer. Delivery takes about one network trip (we assume 10 ms). Idle traffic drops to about 100,000 / 30 = 3,300 requests per second, but each message still costs a fresh request.
steps.idea: Long polling delivers almost instantly over plain HTTP, by parking the request until there is news.
steps.caption: The request is held, then answered the moment news arrives.

steps.title: Server-Sent Events: one long download
steps.body: Server-Sent Events (SSE) make that held response permanent. Bob opens one GET with Accept: text/event-stream. The server never finishes the reply and keeps writing small text events into it. The browser's EventSource reconnects by itself and sends Last-Event-ID so the server can resume. SSE is one-way (server to client) and text-only, which suits feeds and notifications. Bob can still send data with normal POSTs. Notes: EventSource cannot set headers, so authenticate with a cookie or short-lived token. Use HTTP/2, since HTTP/1.1 browsers allow only about 6 connections per site. Make sure proxies do not buffer the stream.
steps.idea: SSE is a one-way push stream over ordinary HTTP, with automatic reconnect and resume built in.
steps.caption: One open response; events flow down it.

steps.title: WebSockets: a two-way pipe
steps.body: A WebSocket starts as a normal HTTP request with an Upgrade header. The server answers 101 Switching Protocols, and the same TCP connection becomes a two-way channel (full-duplex). Either side can now send small frames at any time, each with only a 2 to 14 byte header. In the animation Bob sends a 'typing' frame up and a 'new msg' frame comes down. Delivery is as fast as SSE, about one network trip. The gain is two-way traffic. Unlike EventSource, the browser WebSocket API does not reconnect or resume for you, so your code must. It suits chat, games and shared editing.
steps.idea: A WebSocket upgrades one HTTP connection into a two-way message channel with tiny per-message overhead.
steps.caption: Upgrade handshake first, then frames flow both ways.

steps.title: The gateway remembers who is connected
steps.body: Open connections make servers stateful. In the animation, Bob's socket lives in the memory of one process, Gateway B, and a message can reach Bob only through it. Each idle connection costs roughly 10 to 50 KB of memory (a rule of thumb), so 50,000 connections on one gateway is only 0.5 to 2.5 GB. We assume the 100,000 users are split over two gateways, about 50,000 each. To scale, add gateways. A load balancer only picks a gateway when a connection first opens, so use least-connections routing, and expect a new gateway to start empty.
steps.idea: A connection lives on one specific gateway, so a message cannot be sent from just any server.
steps.caption: Bob is attached to Gateway B only.

steps.title: Delivering across gateways
steps.body: Alice is on Gateway A and Bob on Gateway B. A gateway is the server process that holds client connections. In the animation Alice's message reaches Gateway A, which has the chat service save it first. Then Gateway A publishes it to a pub/sub bus, a shared channel every gateway listens to. The bus gives Gateway B a copy, and B writes it down Bob's socket. Why save first? Simple buses such as Redis Pub/Sub are often at-most-once (a missed message is gone) and keep no replay. A client that reconnects catches up from the saved store.
steps.idea: Save first, then publish. The bus is the fast path, and the store covers anything the bus loses.
steps.caption: Save first, then Gateway A to bus to Gateway B to Bob.

steps.title: A gateway dies
steps.body: Gateway B crashes or is redeployed, and its 50,000 sockets drop at the same instant. If they all reconnect within about a second, that is a burst of 50,000 requests per second. This is a thundering herd: the surviving gateway queues them and delay climbs toward a second. The fix is on the client. Wait a random, growing delay before each retry (exponential backoff with jitter), then send the last message id seen so the server can resume. For planned deploys, drain first: stop accepting new connections, then close old ones gradually.
steps.idea: Connections are fragile. Clients must reconnect after random delays and resume from the last message id.
steps.caption: Gateway B fails and every client rushes to reconnect.

steps.title: Choosing the tool
steps.body: Pick the simplest tool that fits the direction of traffic. Short polling suits rare updates where caching helps, such as a job-status check. SSE suits one-way streams: notifications, prices, live logs. WebSockets suit cases where the client sends often and speed matters: chat, games, shared cursors. Whatever you pick, send a heartbeat (a tiny 'still here' message) every 20 to 30 seconds. Proxies and load balancers cut quiet connections, often after 60 s.
steps.idea: Choose by direction of traffic, and always send heartbeats.
steps.caption: Match the transport to the direction of traffic.

steps.title: From asking to being told
steps.body: HTTP cannot push, so short polling asks often and long polling parks the question. SSE keeps a one-way stream open, and WebSockets give a two-way channel. Open connections pin each user to one gateway, so messages cross gateways through a pub/sub bus, and clients must reconnect with backoff and resume. Durable queues and event logs, which can back this bus, have their own lessons.
steps.idea: Real-time is a held-open connection plus a way to route each message to the gateway that owns it.
steps.caption: Connections at the edge, a bus in the middle.

quiz.q: 100,000 users short-poll every 10 seconds. Roughly how many requests per second does the server see, and what is the average delivery delay?
quiz.why: 100,000 / 10 s = 10,000 requests per second. A message arrives at a random point in the interval, so the average wait is half of it, 5 s.

quiz.q: A live stock ticker only sends prices from server to browser and must reconnect automatically after Wi-Fi drops. Which is the best fit?
options: Long polling with a 5 s timeout
quiz.why: Traffic is one-way, which is exactly what SSE does. EventSource reconnects and resumes with Last-Event-ID built in, so WebSockets add complexity without a benefit.

quiz.q: Alice is on Gateway A and Bob on Gateway B. Why can't Gateway A just write to Bob directly?
options: Bob's socket exists only in Gateway B's memory
The load balancer blocks gateway-to-gateway traffic
Gateways may only talk to the database
quiz.why: A connection is held by one process. Gateway A has no handle for it, so the message must reach Gateway B, usually through a pub/sub bus.

quiz.q: A gateway holding 50,000 sockets restarts and all clients reconnect instantly, overloading the other gateways. What is the standard defence?
options: Switch every client to short polling
Reconnect with exponential backoff plus random jitter
quiz.why: Jitter spreads reconnects over time and backoff slows repeated tries, so the herd arrives gradually instead of as one spike.

quiz.q: A WebSocket works on your laptop but drops after exactly 60 seconds of silence in production. The most likely cause?
options: Browsers cap WebSocket age at 60 s
An idle timeout on a proxy or load balancer closing quiet connections
The server ran out of ports
quiz.why: Intermediaries close connections that carry no traffic. Periodic ping or heartbeat frames every 20 to 30 seconds keep them open.

cheatsheet.def: Client asks on a timer. Simple and cache-friendly, but wasteful when idle, and delay averages half the interval.
Server holds the request until data exists or a timeout (about 30 s), then client re-asks. Low delay over plain HTTP.
One long HTTP response of text events, server to client only. Auto-reconnect and Last-Event-ID resume are built into EventSource.
HTTP Upgrade (101) turns the connection into a full-duplex frame channel. Best when both sides send often.
A server that holds open sockets in memory. Needs a way to route messages to the gateway owning each user.
Gateways subscribe to channels for their users; a publisher reaches every subscribed gateway without knowing who is where.
Retry after a random, growing delay so mass reconnects do not stampede. Pair with a last-seen id to resume.
Small periodic ping (every 20-30 s) that stops proxy idle timeouts and reveals dead peers early.
